_comment: Self-contained demo dataset for the Med-RAG demo console. Two synthetic patients + a small clinical-guidance knowledge base. All data is synthetic — no real PHI. Mirrors the production schema (SQLite facts + FAISS narrative chunks) in one portable file so the demo deploys anywhere in minutes.

chunks.title: Visit 1 — OPD Progress Note
chunks.author: Dr. Kim, General Medicine
chunks.text: Initial consultation. Patient presents with polyuria, fatigue, and elevated fasting glucose. HbA1c measured at 8.4%. Diagnosis: Type 2 Diabetes. Started metformin 500mg twice daily. Dietary counseling provided; referred to nutritionist. Follow-up in 5 weeks.

chunks.title: Visit 2 — OPD Progress Note
chunks.author: Dr. Kim, General Medicine
chunks.text: Follow-up visit. Patient tolerating metformin with mild GI upset, advised to take with meals. HbA1c 8.0%, improved from 8.4%. Fasting glucose trending down. Continue metformin 500mg twice daily. Reinforced dietary plan. Follow-up in 4 weeks.

chunks.title: Visit 3 — OPD Progress Note
chunks.author: Dr. Boyd, General Medicine
chunks.text: Routine follow-up. HbA1c 7.5%, continued improvement. Patient reports better energy levels and adherence to meal plan. Metformin increased to 850mg twice daily to consolidate glycemic control. No acute complications noted. Follow-up in 4 weeks.

chunks.title: Visit 4 — OPD Progress Note
chunks.author: Dr. Kim, General Medicine
chunks.text: Patient reports she stopped taking metformin for approximately two weeks this month due to recurring GI upset. HbA1c 7.7%, slightly up from prior visit. Counseled on extended-release metformin as an alternative; switched to metformin XR 1000mg once daily. Follow-up in 4 weeks.

chunks.title: Visit 5 — OPD Progress Note
chunks.author: Dr. Kim, General Medicine
chunks.text: Follow-up on metformin XR. Patient tolerating the extended-release formulation well, no GI complaints, resumed full adherence. HbA1c 7.2%, best reading to date. Vital signs stable. No acute complications. Continue metformin XR 1000mg daily. Follow-up in 8 weeks.

chunks.title: Visit 1 — Nephrology Consult Note
chunks.author: Dr. Ferreira, Nephrology
chunks.text: Referred for declining renal function. Known Type 2 Diabetes, 11 years. eGFR 54 mL/min (CKD Stage 3a borderline 3b). Current medications: metformin 1000mg twice daily, lisinopril 20mg daily. Urine ACR elevated. Advised strict BP control and repeat renal panel in 3 months.

chunks.title: Visit 2 — OPD Progress Note
chunks.author: Dr. Ferreira, Nephrology
chunks.text: Patient reports self-medicating with over-the-counter ibuprofen for chronic knee pain, roughly 3 times per week for the past month. Advised to stop NSAID use given renal status; discussed paracetamol and topical alternatives. Renal panel ordered ahead of schedule.

chunks.title: Visit 3 — Renal Panel Review
chunks.author: Dr. Ferreira, Nephrology
chunks.text: Repeat renal panel: eGFR 48 mL/min, down from 54 in March — now CKD Stage 3b. Potassium 4.9 mmol/L (upper normal). Patient still on metformin 1000mg twice daily and lisinopril 20mg daily. NSAID cessation reportedly partial. Flagged for medication review at next visit.

chunks.title: Formulary Protocol — Metformin Renal Dosing
chunks.author: Hospital Pharmacy & Therapeutics Committee
chunks.text: Metformin renal dosing protocol: eGFR ≥ 45 — standard dosing. eGFR 30–44 — do not initiate; if already on metformin, reduce to a maximum of 1000mg total daily dose and increase monitoring. eGFR < 30 — metformin is contraindicated; discontinue. Rationale: reduced renal clearance raises the risk of lactic acidosis, a rare but life-threatening complication. Re-check eGFR within 3 months of any downward trend.

chunks.title: Clinical Advisory — NSAIDs in Chronic Kidney Disease
chunks.author: Hospital Pharmacy & Therapeutics Committee
chunks.text: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac) are nephrotoxic and should be avoided in CKD stage 3 and beyond. Combined use of an NSAID with an ACE inhibitor (e.g., lisinopril) and a diuretic — the 'triple whammy' — significantly increases the risk of acute kidney injury. NSAID use can also accelerate eGFR decline and raise serum potassium. Prefer paracetamol or topical agents for analgesia in CKD patients.

chunks.title: Care Standard — Glycemic Targets & Monitoring
chunks.author: Endocrinology Department
chunks.text: General HbA1c target for most adults with Type 2 Diabetes: below 7.0%, individualized for age and comorbidity. HbA1c should be measured every 3 months when therapy has changed or targets are not met, and every 6 months once stable. A downward HbA1c trend across consecutive visits indicates improving glycemic control; interruptions in medication adherence commonly appear as a plateau or rebound in HbA1c.

showcase_queries.label: Drug-safety reasoning
showcase_queries.query: This patient's eGFR has dropped from 54 to 48 and they're still on metformin 1000mg twice daily. What should the care team watch for?
showcase_queries.answer:
Three things stand out for this patient, and each is grounded in his record and the formulary protocols:

**1. Metformin dose is approaching a protocol boundary.** His eGFR is now 48 [1], and the renal dosing protocol caps metformin at 1000mg *total* daily once eGFR falls below 45 [3]. He is currently taking 2000mg/day (1000mg twice daily) [1]. He hasn't crossed the threshold yet, but the trend (54 → 48 in three months [1][2]) means the care team should plan a dose reduction now rather than react later. The underlying risk is lactic acidosis from reduced renal clearance [3].

**2. The NSAID use is likely accelerating the decline.** He reported taking ibuprofen ~3×/week [5], and cessation has only been partial [1]. He is also on lisinopril [2] — an NSAID + ACE-inhibitor combination is specifically flagged as high-risk for acute kidney injury in CKD [4]. Resolving the NSAID issue may be the single highest-impact intervention.

**3. Potassium is at the upper limit.** His potassium is 4.9 [1]; both lisinopril and NSAIDs push potassium upward [4], so the next renal panel should be watched closely.

⚠️ *This is decision support, not a prescription — the medication review already flagged in his chart [1] is where these calls get made.*

showcase_queries.label: Longitudinal trend analysis
showcase_queries.query: Is this patient's glycemic control improving? Summarize the trend across all visits.
showcase_queries.answer:
Yes — overall her control is clearly improving, but the trend is not a straight line, and the dip in the middle is clinically meaningful:

| Visit | Date | HbA1c | What happened |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Jan 14 | 8.4% | Diagnosis; metformin started [1] |
| 2 | Feb 18 | 8.0% | Improving; mild GI upset [2] |
| 3 | Mar 25 | 7.5% | Improving; dose increased [3] |
| 4 | Apr 29 | 7.7% ⚠ | **Rebound** — she stopped metformin for ~2 weeks due to GI side effects [4] |
| 5 | Jun 3 | 7.2% | Best reading; switched to XR formulation, adherence restored [5] |

The visit-4 rebound matches exactly what the care standard predicts: adherence interruptions show up as a plateau or rebound in HbA1c [6]. The clinician's response — switching to extended-release metformin rather than escalating the dose [4] — addressed the *cause* (tolerability) instead of the symptom, and visit 5 confirms it worked [5].

She is not yet at the general target of <7.0% [6], so continued monitoring on the current 8-week cycle is appropriate.

showcase_queries.label: Contradiction check
showcase_queries.query: Did the patient stop taking metformin at any point? Do the records agree?
showcase_queries.answer:
Yes, she did — and the records are **consistent** once read in sequence, though a single-visit read could mislead:

- **Visit 4 (Apr 29)** documents the interruption explicitly: she stopped metformin for approximately two weeks that month due to recurring GI upset [1].
- **Visit 5 (Jun 3)** says she "resumed full adherence" [2] — which only makes sense *because* of the visit-4 interruption. Read alone, visit 5 could imply she never stopped.
- The early warning was there: **visit 2** already noted mild GI upset [3], and visit 3 raised the dose anyway [4], which plausibly worsened tolerability.

So: one interruption, well-documented, resolved by switching to the XR formulation. No contradiction — but this is a good example of why the system retrieves the *full* visit history rather than only the most recent note: longitudinal context is what makes the visit-5 phrasing interpretable.
